turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You think his misfortunes justify his behavior? I think not.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I am astonished by your continued refusal to consider my affections. Your harsh judgments of me in the past, I had hoped, would be tempered by the sincerity of my feelings.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You expect me to forget the way you treated my sister Lydia, and the countless times you looked down on me as inferior? Your feelings are of no consequence to me.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I am astonished by your obstinacy in refusing to acknowledge the depth of my feelings. Your family's inferior social standing and your own lack of refinement are hardly the qualities one would expect to inspire such strong attachment in a gentleman of my standing. You are not, after all, the most impressive or accomplished woman I have ever had the pleasure of meeting.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How dare you imply that my family's station or my own qualities have anything to do with your affections for me? It's clear that you're only interested in me because I'm the sister of the woman you were forced to marry off to a man of lower standing, and you think I'd be a suitable match for you because I'm familiar with that kind of humiliation.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must admit, Miss Bennet, that I find your accusations to be a gross misrepresentation of my character and intentions. My proposal to you was made in sincerity, and I will not be swayed by your unfounded suspicions and prejudices.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be swayed by your empty declarations, Mr. Darcy. I have seen the truth of your character, and I will not be convinced by your words.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Miss Bennet, that you do not judge me by the standards of the inferior society in which you are accustomed to live.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be lectured on propriety by a man who has shown such blatant disregard for the feelings and reputations of those around him, including my own sister.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, I find it quite astonishing that you would stoop to such baseless and personal attacks, Miss Bennet. Your behavior is a far cry from the refined and dignified conduct I have come to expect from a lady of your standing.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You would do well to reflect on your own behavior, Mr. Darcy, before attempting to criticize mine. Your past actions have spoken far louder than any words you've spoken to me, and I see no reason to change my opinion now.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I daresay, Miss Bennet, you would do well to consider the consequences of your refusal, for you may find that my proposal is not so readily dismissed, despite your initial rejection.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must confess, I am astonished that you would think me so foolish as to consider marrying a man who has shown me such disrespect and disdain, simply because he has a fortune and a title.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must admit, Miss Bennet, that I am beginning to tire of your obstinacy, and I warn you, it would be unwise to continue to refuse my proposal, lest you suffer the consequences of your own pride.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not afraid of your consequences, Mr. Darcy, for I would rather live with the knowledge of having made a choice based on principle than to marry a man who has consistently shown me disdain and disrespect.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I find it astonishing that you would so callously dismiss my proposal, considering the esteem in which I hold you, Miss Bennet.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Darcy, it is quite rich of you to speak of esteem, considering the manner in which you have treated me and my family in the past.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I daresay, Miss Bennet, you are mistaken in your assessment of my character. I assure you, my behavior towards you was merely a result of my own sense of what is proper and decent.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be swayed by your attempts to justify your behavior, Mr. Darcy. You have consistently shown a lack of respect for my feelings and opinions, and I see no reason to believe that your actions will change now.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I am beginning to question your judgment, considering the manner in which you are so hastily dismissing my proposal, without affording me the courtesy of a thoughtful consideration.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
